Well, hello doctor. Thank you for taking the time to see me. I, uh, I suppose what brings me in today is... well, it's actually been going on for a little while now, but it's gotten to the point where it's just becoming a real nuisance. We live in a condo over on the east side, and lately, I just find myself... I get stuck, I suppose is the best way to put it. 

I find myself checking things over and over again before I can move on with my day. It’s always the same things, too. I have these boxes in the spare room, and my daily to-do lists, and, well, just the regular drawers around the condo—the kitchen drawers, the dresser, that sort of thing. I'll open one up, look inside, close it, and then... I just have to do it again. I'll open it right back up. And the ridiculous thing is, I know perfectly well I already looked. My memory is fine, I know exactly what's in there and what isn't. But I just can't seem to walk away until I've checked it a few more times. 

My wife will be standing right there by the front door, coat on, just waiting for me to leave it be so we can go out to the store or run our errands, and I'll be standing there pulling the same drawer open for the third or fourth time. I tell her, "Just a minute, just a minute," but it's never just a minute, you know? I just have to do it, even though I know I just looked. It's just very frustrating to deal with, frankly, and she's the one who finally suggested I come talk to someone about it.

Well, yes, actually. Now that you mention it, that's exactly what happens. It's... it's a very nagging sort of feeling, and it just won't leave me be. 

You see, I was a teacher for many years before I retired—middle school, mostly—and over the decades I accumulated quite a lot of materials. I kept a good number of my old teaching files, because, well, you put a lot of work into those things and you just never know what you might want to look back on. But lately, I keep getting these thoughts... these incredibly persistent thoughts that I might have accidentally thrown away something important from those old files. 

Or it happens with my tools, too. We downsized to the condo, so I only kept a small set of tools for minor repairs, hanging pictures, that sort of thing. And I'll suddenly get this thought stuck in my head that I've put a needed tool in the wrong box. I'll be sitting down in my favorite chair—my wife and I usually like to watch a bit of television or read after dinner—and I'll tell myself, "Now, that is highly unlikely. You haven't even touched those teaching files in months, and you know exactly where the hammer is." 

I try to just reason with myself, you know? Because I know it doesn't make logical sense. But even when I tell myself it's unlikely, the thought just comes right back. It just loops around and around in my mind, and it makes it terribly hard to settle down and just enjoy the evening. I'll be sitting there, trying to focus on a book or the program on the screen, and my mind is just absolutely stuck on whether or not a piece of paper from twenty years ago got tossed in the recycling by mistake. It just chatters away at me until I finally get up and go check on it.

Well, no, not really. I mean, I like a tidy house, certainly. We both do. When we downsized and moved into the condo, my wife—she has a wonderful eye for these things, you see—she arranged the living room so nicely, with the armchairs angled just so, and the little side tables matching. I can leave a stack of mail completely askew on the kitchen counter, and as long as I don't have that specific thought that an important paper got accidentally tossed out, I'm perfectly fine leaving it a mess. 

So, no, it doesn't have to be symmetrical or anything like that. I've heard of people who need all their soup cans facing forward in the pantry, or their shoes lined up perfectly by the door, but I've never been quite like that. In fact, if you had seen my desk back when I was teaching middle school, you'd probably laugh—it was a bit of a disaster area, honestly, just stacks of ungraded quizzes and lesson plans everywhere! But I always knew where everything was, at least back then. So, no, the physical arrangement or symmetry of things isn't what's bothering me at all. It's really just those persistent thoughts about misplacing or throwing away something important.

Well, no, not really. I mean, it's not as if I think... oh, I don't know, that the condo is going to catch fire, or that someone in the family is going to fall ill if I don't look in the drawer. It's nothing dramatic like that. My wife actually asked me something very similar just the other week. It's really just... well, it's just about the items themselves. It's that nagging feeling I mentioned before. If I don't check, I just sit there feeling like I've made a foolish mistake. Like I've carelessly tossed out a perfectly good wrench, or one of those old teaching rubrics I spent hours typing up back in the nineties. It's just this incredibly frustrating sense of... of uncertainty, I suppose. I just want to be absolutely, one hundred percent sure that I haven't made an error. 

So I wouldn't say I'm preventing a catastrophe or anything terrible. It's just that if I don't go back and look, that thought—that I might have misplaced something—just gets louder and louder until I can't concentrate on a single other thing. I'll just be sitting there stewing over it. I just have to see the item with my own eyes to prove to myself that it's still there, even though, as I said, I already know it is! It's quite the paradox, really, when you think about it. But no, no impending doom or anything of that sort. Just trying to quiet my own mind, I suppose.

I tell her, \"Just a minute, just a minute,\" but it's never just a minute, you know? I just have to do it, even though I know I just looked. It's just very frustrating to deal with, frankly, and she's the one who finally suggested I come talk to someone about it.\n\nDoctor: Do you have any disturbing or intrusive thoughts that keep repeating in your mind?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, actually. Now that you mention it, that's exactly what happens. I kept a good number of my old teaching files, because, well, you put a lot of work into those things and you just never know what you might want to look back on. But lately, I keep getting these thoughts... these incredibly persistent thoughts that I might have accidentally thrown away something important from those old files. \n\nOr it happens with my tools, too. Well... you know, it's funny you ask that, because it's not quite as simple as just feeling less anxious. I mean, yes, in the immediate moment, there is a certain... relief, I suppose you could call it. It's like scratching an itch. When I finally get up from my chair—which is quite a comfortable chair, mind you, a nice leather recliner my daughter got me for my seventieth birthday—and I walk over to the closet or the filing cabinet, and I actually lay my eyes on the hammer or the old lesson plans... yes, the nagging thought stops for a moment. 

But the relief, it's so incredibly fleeting. It's almost frustrating how short-lived it is. Because I'll close the drawer, feeling like, "Okay, good, it's there, I didn't throw it away." And I'll walk back to the living room. But sometimes, before I've even sat back down, or maybe five minutes after I pick my book back up, the thought just creeps right back in. "Are you sure you saw it? Maybe it was a different file. Maybe you just imagined seeing the hammer." 

So, I wouldn't say I feel *less anxious* overall. If anything, the whole process is exhausting. I'll check it, feel a tiny bit better for a split second, and then the doubt just washes right back over me. It's like trying to bail out a leaky boat with a teaspoon. You think you're making progress, but the water just keeps coming back in. So, no, the checking doesn't really fix the anxiety in any meaningful way. It just sort of... pauses it for a second before the whole cycle starts up again.

Oh, goodness... well, that is a... that's a rather difficult question to answer, isn't it? Because, you see, I'm honestly not sure. I really don't know. But if, say, one of our grandkids comes over to visit and bumps a lamp out of place, or if the coasters on the coffee table aren't perfectly lined up, it doesn't bother me in the slightest. \n\nI don't get that... that nagging feeling about things being uneven or out of order. It's really just the checking of the boxes and the drawers that I mentioned earlier. I can leave a stack of mail completely askew on the kitchen counter, and as long as I don't have that specific thought that an important paper got accidentally tossed out, I'm perfectly fine leaving it a mess. \n\nSo, no, it doesn't have to be symmetrical or anything like that. I've heard of people who need all their soup cans facing forward in the pantry, or their shoes lined up perfectly by the door, but I've never been quite like that. In fact, if you had seen my desk back when I was teaching middle school, you'd probably laugh—it was a bit of a disaster area, honestly, just stacks of ungraded quizzes and lesson plans everywhere! But I always knew where everything was, at least back then. So, no, the physical arrangement or symmetry of things isn't what's bothering me at all. It's really just those persistent thoughts about misplacing or throwing away something important.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like checking these things repeatedly is preventing something bad from happening?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. I mean, it's not as if I think... oh, I don't know, that the condo is going to catch fire, or that someone in the family is going to fall ill if I don't look in the drawer. It's nothing dramatic like that. My wife actually asked me something very similar just the other week. We were getting ready to head over to the grocery store—the one down on 4th street, they have those wonderful fresh bakery items on Tuesday mornings—and I was stuck checking the hall table drawer. She sighed and asked me, \"What on earth do you think is going to happen if you don't look in there again?\" And I had to tell her, honestly, nothing! Nothing bad is going to happen at all. \n\nIt's really just... well, it's just about the items themselves. It's that nagging feeling I mentioned before. If I don't check, I just sit there feeling like I've made a foolish mistake. Like I've carelessly tossed out a perfectly good wrench, or one of those old teaching rubrics I spent hours typing up back in the nineties. It's just this incredibly frustrating sense of... of uncertainty, I suppose. I just want to be absolutely, one hundred percent sure that I haven't made an error. \n\nSo I wouldn't say I'm preventing a catastrophe or anything terrible. I'll just be sitting there stewing over it. I just have to see the item with my own eyes to prove to myself that it's still there, even though, as I said, I already know it is! It's quite the paradox, really, when you think about it. But no, no impending doom or anything of that sort. Just trying to quiet my own mind, I suppose.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel less anxious after you've checked these things repeatedly?\n\nPatient: Well... you know, it's funny you ask that, because it's not quite as simple as just feeling less anxious. I mean, yes, in the immediate moment, there is a certain... relief, I suppose you could call it. It's like scratching an itch. Maybe you just imagined seeing the hammer.\" \n\nSo, I wouldn't say I feel *less anxious* overall. If anything, the whole process is exhausting. I'll check it, feel a tiny bit better for a split second, and then the doubt just washes right back over me. It's like trying to bail out a leaky boat with a teaspoon. You think you're making progress, but the water just keeps coming back in. So, no, the checking doesn't really fix the anxiety in any meaningful way. Don't go look. Just ignore it and it will pass.\" So I tried. I really did try to just stop checking, right then and there. But... would the anxiety decrease if I could somehow permanently stop? I just don't know, because in that moment, sitting there trying not to check, the worry just built up and built up. It was like a kettle on the stove, just getting hotter and hotter until it whistles. I couldn't focus on the television screen at all, couldn't hear a single word the narrator was saying about Yosemite. I just kept picturing that bill sitting in the blue bin out in the garage, getting ruined. \n\nSo, if I were somehow magically able to just stop doing the checking altogether... I don't know if my mind would finally quiet down and I'd feel peaceful, or if I'd just be sitting in my armchair vibrating with all that pent-up uncertainty all day long. It's a bit of a mystery to me, frankly, because I've never actually been able to hold out long enough to find out! I always end up getting up and looking eventually, just to break the tension. Well, no, not really. I mean, harm? No, no, it's nothing like that. It's not as if I think someone is going to get hurt, or the house is going to collapse because I can't find a particular socket wrench or a stack of old papers. It's really just... well, it's just the principle of the thing, I suppose. 

Take those old lesson plans, for example. The ones I was telling you about from the nineties. Now, I haven't taught a class in over a decade, and I certainly don't have any pressing need for a rubric on a sophomore history essay about the Industrial Revolution. But the thought of it just being gone... of me having accidentally thrown it away without realizing it... it just feels like such a foolish, careless mistake. It's not dangerous, it's just... it's just wrong. 

And it's the same with the tools. My wife—she's a saint, really, putting up with me—she'll say, "Arthur, if you really need a Phillips head screwdriver that badly, we can just go down to the Ace Hardware on Main Street and buy another one for three dollars." And she's absolutely right, of course she is. It wouldn't be the end of the world. It wouldn't cause any harm to anyone. But in my mind, it's just this nagging, persistent feeling that I've lost something perfectly good, something I might need someday, however unlikely that is. It's the uncertainty of it all, the feeling of not being completely in control of my own belongings. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm worried about any sort of harm or danger. It's just... well, it's just incredibly bothersome, is what it is.

Well, yes and no, I suppose. It's... it's a bit complicated. I mean, yes, on some level, I suppose I am trying to prevent a mistake—the mistake of having thrown something away or misplaced it. But really, what brought me in to see you in the first place, what finally made me realize I needed to talk to someone, is just the sheer repetition of it all.

Well, I suppose it’s a bit of both, isn't it? But if I had to really put my finger on it, it's... it's the uncertainty that just gnaws at me. The uncertainty that I might have made a mistake. It’s this... this incessant, nagging thought that just pops into my head, usually right when I'm trying to relax. 

Just yesterday, for instance, I was sitting in my favorite armchair—it’s a wonderful old leather thing, terribly comfortable, my wife wanted to throw it out when we moved into the condo but I simply wouldn't let her—anyway, I was sitting there, reading the morning paper, and suddenly the thought just arrives out of nowhere: "Arthur, did you accidentally toss out that file on the 1994 curriculum changes?" 

Now, I know, logically, I haven't looked at that file in years. I know it’s highly unlikely I would have even had it out of the filing cabinet, let alone thrown it away. But the thought just... sticks. It’s like a burr caught in your sock when you’re out for a walk in the woods. You try to ignore it, you try to just keep walking, but it just keeps pricking at you. 

I tell myself, "Arthur, don't be ridiculous, it's fine." But the thought just circles back around. Or I'll think, "Did I put that good socket wrench in the box with the gardening supplies instead of the toolbox?" And even though I know I wouldn't do something so silly, I just can't settle down. I can't finish reading my article on the local mayoral race, I can't enjoy my cup of tea... because the thought just keeps echoing, over and over, until I finally give in and go out to the garage to check. So yes, it’s those nagging thoughts, that terrible uncertainty that I might have done something foolish with my old teaching files or my tools, that just makes it utterly impossible to sit still and be at peace.

I can leave a stack of mail completely askew on the kitchen counter, and as long as I don't have that specific thought that an important paper got accidentally tossed out, I'm perfectly fine leaving it a mess. \n\nSo, no, it doesn't have to be symmetrical or anything like that. I've heard of people who need all their soup cans facing forward in the pantry, or their shoes lined up perfectly by the door, but I've never been quite like that. In fact, if you had seen my desk back when I was teaching middle school, you'd probably laugh—it was a bit of a disaster area, honestly, just stacks of ungraded quizzes and lesson plans everywhere! But I always knew where everything was, at least back then. So, no, the physical arrangement or symmetry of things isn't what's bothering me at all. It's really just those persistent thoughts about misplacing or throwing away something important.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like checking these things repeatedly is preventing something bad from happening?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. I mean, it's not as if I think... oh, I don't know, that the condo is going to catch fire, or that someone in the family is going to fall ill if I don't look in the drawer. It's nothing dramatic like that. My wife actually asked me something very similar just the other week. We were getting ready to head over to the grocery store—the one down on 4th street, they have those wonderful fresh bakery items on Tuesday mornings—and I was stuck checking the hall table drawer. She sighed and asked me, \"What on earth do you think is going to happen if you don't look in there again?\" And I had to tell her, honestly, nothing! Nothing bad is going to happen at all. \n\nIt's really just... well, it's just about the items themselves. It's that nagging feeling I mentioned before. If I don't check, I just sit there feeling like I've made a foolish mistake. Like I've carelessly tossed out a perfectly good wrench, or one of those old teaching rubrics I spent hours typing up back in the nineties. It's just this incredibly frustrating sense of... of uncertainty, I suppose. I just want to be absolutely, one hundred percent sure that I haven't made an error. \n\nSo I wouldn't say I'm preventing a catastrophe or anything terrible. It's just that if I don't go back and look, that thought—that I might have misplaced something—just gets louder and louder until I can't concentrate on a single other thing. I'll just be sitting there stewing over it. I just have to see the item with my own eyes to prove to myself that it's still there, even though, as I said, I already know it is! It's quite the paradox, really, when you think about it. But no, no impending doom or anything of that sort. Just trying to quiet my own mind, I suppose.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel less anxious after you've checked these things repeatedly?\n\nPatient: Well... you know, it's funny you ask that, because it's not quite as simple as just feeling less anxious. I mean, yes, in the immediate moment, there is a certain... relief, I suppose you could call it. It's like scratching an itch. When I finally get up from my chair—which is quite a comfortable chair, mind you, a nice leather recliner my daughter got me for my seventieth birthday—and I walk over to the closet or the filing cabinet, and I actually lay my eyes on the hammer or the old lesson plans... yes, the nagging thought stops for a moment. \n\nBut the relief, it's so incredibly fleeting. It's almost frustrating how short-lived it is. Because I'll close the drawer, feeling like, \"Okay, good, it's there, I didn't throw it away.\" And I'll walk back to the living room. But sometimes, before I've even sat back down, or maybe five minutes after I pick my book back up, the thought just creeps right back in. \"Are you sure you saw it? Maybe it was a different file. Maybe you just imagined seeing the hammer.\" \n\nSo, I wouldn't say I feel *less anxious* overall. If anything, the whole process is exhausting. I'll check it, feel a tiny bit better for a split second, and then the doubt just washes right back over me. It's like trying to bail out a leaky boat with a teaspoon. You think you're making progress, but the water just keeps coming back in. So, no, the checking doesn't really fix the anxiety in any meaningful way. It just sort of... pauses it for a second before the whole cycle starts up again.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you could stop checking these things, your anxiety would decrease?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness... well, that is a... that's a rather difficult question to answer, isn't it? Because, you see, I'm honestly not sure. I really don't know. My wife is always telling me—just last week we were sitting down to watch a program, one of those wonderful Ken Burns documentaries on PBS, the one about the National Parks, which is just stunningly filmed by the way, you really ought to see it if you haven't—and I had this sudden thought that I had accidentally tossed the electric bill into the recycling bin along with the weekly grocery circulars. \n\nAnd she said to me, \"Just sit here. Don't go look. Just ignore it and it will pass.\" So I tried. I really did try to just stop checking, right then and there. But... would the anxiety decrease if I could somehow permanently stop? I just don't know, because in that moment, sitting there trying not to check, the worry just built up and built up. It was like a kettle on the stove, just getting hotter and hotter until it whistles. I couldn't focus on the television screen at all, couldn't hear a single word the narrator was saying about Yosemite. I just kept picturing that bill sitting in the blue bin out in the garage, getting ruined. \n\nSo, if I were somehow magically able to just stop doing the checking altogether... I don't know if my mind would finally quiet down and I'd feel peaceful, or if I'd just be sitting in my armchair vibrating with all that pent-up uncertainty all day long. It's a bit of a mystery to me, frankly, because I've never actually been able to hold out long enough to find out! I always end up getting up and looking eventually, just to break the tension. So, yes, I really couldn't say for certain one way or the other what would happen if I just stopped.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the things you check for could potentially cause harm if they were missing or misplaced?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. I mean, harm? No, no, it's nothing like that. It's not as if I think someone is going to get hurt, or the house is going to collapse because I can't find a particular socket wrench or a stack of old papers. It's really just... well, it's just the principle of the thing, I suppose. \n\nTake those old lesson plans, for example. The ones I was telling you about from the nineties. Now, I haven't taught a class in over a decade, and I certainly don't have any pressing need for a rubric on a sophomore history essay about the Industrial Revolution. But the thought of it just being gone... of me having accidentally thrown it away without realizing it... it just feels like such a foolish, careless mistake. It's not dangerous, it's just... it's just wrong. \n\nAnd it's the same with the tools. My wife—she's a saint, really, putting up with me—she'll say, \"Arthur, if you really need a Phillips head screwdriver that badly, we can just go down to the Ace Hardware on Main Street and buy another one for three dollars.\" And she's absolutely right, of course she is. It wouldn't be the end of the world. It wouldn't cause any harm to anyone. But in my mind, it's just this nagging, persistent feeling that I've lost something perfectly good, something I might need someday, however unlikely that is. It's the uncertainty of it all, the feeling of not being completely in control of my own belongings. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm worried about any sort of harm or danger. It's just... well, it's just incredibly bothersome, is what it is.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're trying to prevent a mistake from happening when you check these things repeatedly?\n\nPatient: Well, yes and no, I suppose. I know the hammer is in the drawer, or the papers are in the box. I had to go back into the guest room and check the filing cabinet one more time, just to be absolutely certain I hadn't accidentally mixed up the tax documents with the old lesson plans. I knew I hadn't. But I had to look. So it's less about preventing a mistake in the future, and more about... just needing to satisfy this terrible, repetitive urge before I can physically allow myself to move on with my day, even when I know it's completely unnecessary and I'm keeping my poor wife waiting.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your checking behavior is more about avoiding the feeling of uncertainty or the feeling of having made a mistake?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose it’s a bit of both, isn't it? Well, control... I suppose you could use that word, but honestly, it doesn't really feel like control. It feels more like being controlled, if I'm being perfectly frank. It's almost frustrating how short-lived it is. Because I'll close the drawer, feeling like, \"Okay, good, it's there, I didn't throw it away.\" And I'll walk back to the living room. But sometimes, before I've even sat back down, or maybe five minutes after I pick my book back up, the thought just creeps right back in. \"Are you sure you saw it? Maybe it was a different file. Maybe you just imagined seeing the hammer.\" \n\nSo, I wouldn't say I feel *less anxious* overall. If anything, the whole process is exhausting. I'll check it, feel a tiny bit better for a split second, and then the doubt just washes right back over me. It's like trying to bail out a leaky boat with a teaspoon. You think you're making progress, but the water just keeps coming back in. So, no, the checking doesn't really fix the anxiety in any meaningful way. It just sort of... pauses it for a second before the whole cycle starts up again.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you could stop checking these things, your anxiety would decrease?\n\nPatient: Oh, goodness... well, that is a... that's a rather difficult question to answer, isn't it? Because, you see, I'm honestly not sure. I really don't know. My wife is always telling me—just last week we were sitting down to watch a program, one of those wonderful Ken Burns documentaries on PBS, the one about the National Parks, which is just stunningly filmed by the way, you really ought to see it if you haven't—and I had this sudden thought that I had accidentally tossed the electric bill into the recycling bin along with the weekly grocery circulars. \n\nAnd she said to me, \"Just sit here. Don't go look. Just ignore it and it will pass.\" So I tried. I really did try to just stop checking, right then and there. But... would the anxiety decrease if I could somehow permanently stop? I couldn't focus on the television screen at all, couldn't hear a single word the narrator was saying about Yosemite. I just kept picturing that bill sitting in the blue bin out in the garage, getting ruined. \n\nSo, if I were somehow magically able to just stop doing the checking altogether... I don't know if my mind would finally quiet down and I'd feel peaceful, or if I'd just be sitting in my armchair vibrating with all that pent-up uncertainty all day long. It's a bit of a mystery to me, frankly, because I've never actually been able to hold out long enough to find out! I always end up getting up and looking eventually, just to break the tension. So, yes, I really couldn't say for certain one way or the other what would happen if I just stopped.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the things you check for could potentially cause harm if they were missing or misplaced?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. It's just... well, it's just incredibly bothersome, is what it is.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're trying to prevent a mistake from happening when you check these things repeatedly?\n\nPatient: Well, yes and no, I suppose. Well, Doctor, I feel like we might be splitting hairs a bit here, because whether you want to label it as a fear of making a mistake or just the pure, agonizing uncertainty of it all, it all leads back to the exact same place. I have to check it again before I can move on. I simply cannot walk away. And the sheer ridiculousness of it all, the part that makes me feel like I'm losing my mind, is that I know perfectly well I already looked! I know it! I can picture the contents of the drawer perfectly. But I just can't stop, even when my wife is standing right there in the hallway, purse in hand, just waiting for me to just leave it be so we can get on with our afternoon. So, you see, you can call it a fear of a mistake, or you can call it the uncertainty of not knowing, but the real issue, the thing that is completely exhausting me and holding up poor Helen, is the checking itself.
